STR TURNOVER CREW PLANNER · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Ten turnovers, two crews: which cleans should you take today?

Booking turnovers in the order owners ask, or the biggest fee first, fills the day with the wrong work. Paste the queue — fee, supplies, clean minutes, the checkout and the next check-in and where each unit is — and get the exact set of cleans with the highest profit for the day, which crew does each and in what order, the drive and idle time it implies, what each turnover it declines would need to pay, and what first-come booking leaves behind.

For vacation-rental cleaning companies and property managers. Nothing is uploaded: the text box is analysed in this browser and never leaves your device.

    Prefer a CLI?

    Same logic, zero dependencies, one command — reads a file or stdin:

    node cli.mjs plan turnovers.csv --crews 2 --start 09:00 --end 18:00 --hourly 40 --json
cat turnovers.csv | node cli.mjs plan - --crews 3 --speed 25

    Get cli.mjs and engine.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install, no network call. More: Is a second cleaning crew worth it? Checkout windows and drive-time math.

    What's recognised

    InputHandling

    The plan is exact for the numbers you type (a search over every set, order and split across crews, up to 12 turnovers and 3 identical crews). One depot; real traffic, parking, crews of different speed or pay, early check-ins, owner cancellations, laundry pickup and the value of a long-term client are not modelled. Distance is straight-line miles times your circuity factor, not a routing service.

    Common questions

    Does it upload my turnover list?

    No. The browser page works on the text you paste, in your own browser, and never sends it anywhere. The CLI reads a local file or stdin and makes no network call.

    How is the best day found?

    For one crew it searches over which turnovers have been done and which was last, keeping every way to get there that is not both later and less profitable than another. It then tries every way to split the queue across your crews. That finds the exact best plan for the numbers you give, and the tests compare it with trying every assignment and every order.

    Why would it turn down a turnover I would normally take?

    Because a crew can only be in one place. A clean that pays well but drives you across the map, or sits in a window that collides with two better cleans, can cost more than the two it displaces. The tool says what the turnover would need to pay to earn its place.

    Where do the costs come from?

    From your own books: fuel and wear per mile, and what an hour of one crew costs you in wages and payroll cost. They are your estimates, so treat the plan as a decision aid, not a forecast.

    Who is it for?

    Vacation-rental cleaning companies and property managers with one to three crews choosing which of the day's turnovers to take and who does them.

It chooses between options using the numbers you supply; it is not a forecast of what will happen on the day.

is-a-second-cleaning-crew-worth-it.html.text:
STR Turnover Crew Planner · guide

Is a second cleaning crew worth it? Checkout windows and drive-time math

Short answer: a crew earns its place when the turnovers it adds, after supplies, clean time, the drive between units and the dead time waiting for checkouts, pay more than the crew costs. Checkout and check-in windows decide how many turnovers one crew can physically reach, so the answer is a property of the day's queue, not of the business.

A worked queue

Ten turnovers, crews leaving a depot at 09:00 and due back at 18:00, each crew costing $40 an hour while driving or cleaning and $0.70 a mile, driving 30 mph over roads 1.3 times the straight-line distance. Fees run from $85 for a studio to $300 for a linen-heavy penthouse.

  • One crew takes 3 turnovers for $119.13 over 31.4 miles. Booking in the order owners asked would have earned only $32.70, and the biggest fees first $90.94.
  • Two crews take 6 turnovers for $214.41 over 52.6 miles, $95.29 more than one. That is $138.92 more than the better of first-come and biggest-fee-first booking, which fill the two crews with $75.49 and $62.04 days.
  • Three crews take 8 turnovers for $245.43 over 107.3 miles, only $31.02 more than two: the third crew spends most of its day driving between far units.

With two crews the planner declines the $210 Pine Cabin, the $240 Harbor 3BR, the $260 Ski Chalet and the $175 Mill Cottage. Each would earn a place only at a higher fee: about $258.89, $271.03, $336.11 and $208.24 respectively. Those are the quotes to give an owner, not the fees asked.

What to feed it

  1. Crew cost per hour: wages and payroll cost for the whole crew divided by hours actually worked, not hours paid.
  2. Per-mile cost: fuel plus tires and maintenance per mile driven.
  3. For each turnover, the checkout and the next check-in from your calendar, and the miles east and north from your depot.

Check any management contract first: some require you to service certain units, and a guest arriving to an unfinished clean costs more than any optimum saves.

Questions

Is a second cleaning crew worth it?

It is worth it when the extra turnovers it can take clear the crew's cost after the drive and the idle time between checkouts. On the worked queue a second crew lifts the day from $119.13 to $214.41, a gain of $95.29, but a third lifts it only $31.02 more, so the third is worth it only if its cost for the hours it works is below that.

How do I decide which turnovers to take on a busy checkout day?

Compare whole days, not single cleans: for a set of turnovers, each crew's order, add what each pays after supplies and clean time, subtract the drive between them and check each window. The best day is the best such split. The planner finds it exactly for up to 12 turnovers and 3 crews.

What should a turnover pay to be worth a detour?

The planner prints, for each turnover it declines, the fee at which the best day would include it. Quote that for a far or tight-window unit, or use it as the floor when an owner asks for a discount.

No warranty. This guide is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind. It is not financial, tax, legal or business advice, and you are responsible for verifying its output, for the numbers you enter, and for any management contract that obliges you to take a turnover. The worked example is illustrative arithmetic, not a forecast.
